statement: In dried cannabis flower that licensed growers sent for state compliance testing to six commercial laboratories in six US states (Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington; December 2013 to January 2021; 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results), the Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category that one consumer cannabis website's strain database links to each strain name, matched by name to the growers' own sample names (so the category is the website's, not necessarily what each package said; 73.4% of samples could be given one), was barely related to the samples' terpene profiles, the mix of the compounds the authors describe as responsible for cannabis's smell (Smith et al., 2022). THC and CBD content were not compared between the categories, and no effects on people were measured. In the 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results, a score of how much more samples resemble others with the same label than samples with the nearest other label (the silhouette score, from −1 to 1) averaged −0.03 for the categories, with most samples below zero, against 0.27 when samples were grouped by their most abundant terpene and 0.38 for three groups found by a clustering method in the same terpene data, which the authors expected to separate better; the category analysis also counted 12,322 samples (29.9%) that had no category as a group of their own. Strain names carried more information: for 26 of the 41 names attached to at least five growers with at least five samples each, products sold under the same name by different growers were more alike in terpene profile than names shuffled at random, 13 did not differ from chance and 2 (LSD and Durban Poison) were less alike than chance (editors' count of the significance marks in the paper's figure); even randomly paired products were fairly similar, at about 0.69 on a 0-to-1 similarity scale (read from the figure). Among 12,063 THC-dominant products with a category, Sativa products made up 30.9% of the terpinolene-rich group against 15.0% overall, yet that group was still mostly Hybrid (55.8%), and the test the paper reports for this appears to have been computed on percentages rather than counts (editors' calculation). The six laboratories' methods were not standardized, which the authors say prevents them from separating laboratory from regional differences, and the corresponding author is employed by the website that supplied the categories and strain names. In a small Dutch study, two cultivars that a seed company's website describes as Sativa-dominant (Amnesia) and Indica-dominant (White Widow), bought at ten coffee shops in four cities on two visits about two months apart (35 samples), differed in terpenes and minor cannabinoids but had similar THC (about 17% and 16% of the weight); many compounds varied by more than 25% between purchases of the same name, 3 samples had the chemistry of the other cultivar and were left out as presumed mix-ups, and of three pharmacy varieties one, bred from a variety with a large share of Sativa genes, resembled the Indica-dominant cultivar (Hazekamp & Fischedick, 2012; no statistical tests; the first author worked for the grower of the pharmacy varieties). Neither study measured how the products felt, so neither can say whether the labels predict effects. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do indica and sativa labels tell you what's in your weed? Mostly not. In lab tests of 41,201 THC-rich flower samples from six US states, samples that a strain website calls indica, hybrid or sativa were mixed together in their terpenes, the compounds behind weed's smell: on average, a sample was about as close to another label's samples as to its own. Strain names did somewhat better: for 26 of 41 common names, products from different growers were more alike than chance, but for 13 they were not, and 2 names were less alike than chance. Sativa labels were twice as common among terpinolene-rich products, though even there most were labelled hybrid. The study compared only these smell compounds, not THC or CBD, used the website's labels rather than the packages, and measured no effects on people. A small Dutch study found that two coffee-shop strains, one described as sativa-type and one as indica-type, differed in terpenes but had similar THC, and varied a lot from purchase to purchase.
population: Dried female cannabis flower submitted by licensed growers (3,319 producers) for state compliance testing at six commercial laboratories in Alaska, California, Florida, Michigan, Oregon and Washington, December 2013 to January 2021: 89,923 samples after cleaning, 42,843 with terpene results, 41,201 THC-dominant samples with terpene results in the label analysis, and 13,401 THC-dominant products (one producer's samples under one name, averaged), 12,063 of them with a category; 41 strain names in the name analysis. Also 35 samples of two cultivars bought at ten Dutch coffee shops in four cities (purchase dates not given; paper received November 2011) and three Dutch pharmacy varieties
exposure: The Indica, Hybrid or Sativa category and the popular strain name that a consumer cannabis website's strain database attaches to each name, matched to growers' sample names by string matching and an expert dictionary of name variants (not read from packages); in the Dutch study, the name under which a sample was bought and each cultivar's Sativa or Indica background as given by a seed company's website
comparator: Samples with other categories or names; groupings built from the same terpene data (each sample's most abundant terpene; three clusters found by k-means); names shuffled at random across growers (200 repetitions); in the Dutch study, the other cultivar and three pharmacy varieties grown under controlled conditions
outcome: How closely samples sharing a label resembled each other in terpene profile (silhouette score; cosine similarity between growers' products against shuffled names; share of a name's products in its most common terpene cluster; category shares by cluster); in the Dutch study, separation of the two cultivars in a principal component analysis of 28 compounds, THC content and variation between purchases. No effects on people were measured
magnitude: Smith et al. (2022), THC-dominant samples with terpene results (n = 41,201): mean silhouette score −0.03 for the Indica/Hybrid/Sativa category (groups: Hybrid 17,616, no category 12,322, Indica 6,681, Sativa 4,582), 0.27 for the dominant terpene and 0.38 for three k-means clusters; differences |d′| = 3.49 (k-means against category), 1.83 (dominant terpene against category) and 0.54 (k-means against dominant terpene), all P < 0.0001; no intervals. Clusters: I (caryophyllene-limonene) 21,811 (52.9%), II (myrcene-pinene) 14,188 (34.4%), III (terpinolene-myrcene) 5,202 (12.6%). Strain names (41): more consistent than shuffled names for 26, no different for 13, less consistent for 2 (LSD, Durban Poison) (editors' count of the Fig 8C significance marks; the text gives one test for the majority of names, P < 0.0001, |d′| = 1.44 as printed); shuffled baseline about 0.69 cosine similarity (read from Fig 8C); Purple Punch 96% of products in one cluster against 61.8% expected under shuffling, Tangie 62.5% in its most common cluster. Category shares among 12,063 products with a category (editors' sum of the Fig 9A legend): overall Hybrid 60.6%, Indica 24.4%, Sativa 15.0%; Cluster III Hybrid 55.8%, Indica 13.3%, Sativa 30.9% (χ² 22.2, P < 0.0001 as printed); editors' calculation: the χ² formula applied to the Fig 9B percentages as if they were counts gives 22.3 for Cluster III and 1.2 and 0.6 for Clusters I and II, which the paper reports as not different. Hazekamp & Fischedick (2012): THC 167.5 mg/g (SD 21.88) in Amnesia against 159.5 (SD 26.76) in White Widow, reported as not significantly different with no test shown; myrcene 0.7 against 2.9 mg/g; terpinolene 1.9 mg/g in Amnesia, not detected in White Widow; relative standard deviation above 25% for 14 compounds as printed (editors' count of Table 1: 14 compound-and-cultivar pairs, 13 distinct compounds); 3 of 35 samples bought under one name matched the other cultivar.

risk_of_bias.note: Not rated down separately: the category result rests on 41,201 samples and is visible in the raw scatter (Fig 6A). Unstandardized methods across six laboratories and repeat submissions by the same producer add noise and dependence, and the cluster χ² and some effect sizes are unreliable (card sc_smith_2022, JBI moderate), but these weaken the secondary associations, which the statement words with their limits. The Dutch study is at high risk of bias (small unsystematic sample, post hoc exclusions, no tests, a conflict of interest; card sc_hazekamp_2012) and only qualifies the claim.

inconsistency.note: The Dutch study points the same way on variation within names, and on THC not telling its two cultivars apart; with two cultivars it cannot test the categories in general.

indirectness.note: Rated down one level: the categories tested are those a consumer website's database attaches to strain names, matched by name, not the labels printed on packages or given at sale; only terpenes were compared, not THC or CBD; the products are compliance-tested flower from six US states in 2013–2021; and nothing about effects was measured, although effects are what people usually mean by the labels.

imprecision.note: A very large sample for the category result; no intervals are printed, but the score sits near zero by a wide margin. The name results rest on 41 names and are given as counts.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one analysis of laboratory records; the cleaned data and code are stated to be public.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claim: never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: Descriptive analysis of product records (cross-sectional): starts low; indirectness −1 (website categories matched by name, terpenes only, US compliance-tested flower in 2013–2021, no effects), which gives very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded. 'Describes' because the claim reports how labels and chemistry line up in products, not an effect on people. The central finding, that the categories barely separate terpene profiles, is firmer than the secondary ones: the strain-name counts are the editors' count of figure marks (the paper gives one summary test, and the recount agrees with the first reader's), and the Sativa-terpinolene association rests on a test that appears to use percentages. The claim does not adopt the authors' conclusions about effects and marketing, which go beyond the chemistry measured, nor the Dutch study's estimate that 20% of coffee-shop visits gave an unreliable product, which counts presumed mix-ups the authors concede may be genuine. Status single study: the Dutch study tested two cultivars and qualifies the claim; the earlier label studies the US paper describes were not read.

statement: In family members (mostly women: spouses, partners and parents) of adults with alcohol or other drug problems who refused treatment, training the family member in CRAFT (community reinforcement and family training; in the largest trial about 12 hours of individual sessions with a therapist, teaching ways to reward not drinking, to communicate, to handle dangerous situations and to suggest treatment) compared with twelve-step family approaches increases the share of relatives who enter treatment, in four small US randomized trials published 1986–2002, three of them from the groups that developed CRAFT and its first version. In the largest trial (130 family members in Albuquerque, USA, 91% women, living with a relative with a drinking problem and seeing them on at least 40% of days; Miller et al., 1999), the relative entered treatment within 6 months (at least an assessment and one session) in 29 of 45 cases (64 in 100) after CRAFT, 12 of 40 (30 in 100) after a Johnson Institute intervention, which prepares the family for a group confrontation, and 6 of 45 (13 in 100) after Al-Anon facilitation, up to 12 individual sessions encouraging involvement in Al-Anon, which the authors note is not the same as a simple referral to Al-Anon; in the Johnson group, 70 in 100 families chose not to hold the confrontation, and 9 of the 12 that did saw their relative enter treatment. Across the four trials (two on alcohol, two on illicit drugs, cocaine most often), relatives entered treatment in 84 of 125 CRAFT cases (67 in 100) against 18 of 99 with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches (18 in 100): relative risk 3.25 (95% CI 2.11 to 5.02), with every trial pointing the same way (I² 2.9%; Roozen et al., 2010); the comparison with the Johnson intervention rests on the one trial (relative risk 2.15, 1.28 to 3.62), which the review's discussion calls almost three times as effective. Family members' own depression, anger and family relationships improved over 6 months by similar amounts in all three groups of the largest trial, whether or not the relative entered treatment; with no group left without help, no approach can be credited with that improvement, and the review's pooled 'improvement' compares scores before and after within the CRAFT groups only. The trials counted whether the relative started treatment, not drinking or drug use, which the largest trial reports separately (not read here), or safety; relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use were excluded from the largest trial; family members and therapists knew which approach they had; therapists were not crossed with approaches (in the largest trial, CRAFT's less experienced therapists were supervised by the approach's developer, a co-author); and the review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 on its study card (no protocol, no list of excluded studies, no trial-by-trial risk-of-bias judgments, no check for unpublished trials). Certainty: moderate, for treatment entry against twelve-step family approaches. Status: replicated.
plain: Can family members help get someone who refuses treatment into it? A skills course for families called CRAFT did better than the other approaches tested. In the biggest trial, with 130 family members of people with drinking problems, 64 in 100 relatives started treatment within 6 months after CRAFT, against 30 in 100 after training for a family confrontation (7 in 10 of those families decided not to hold it) and 13 in 100 after counselling aimed at joining Al-Anon. Across four small US trials, two about alcohol and two about other drugs, relatives started treatment about 3 times as often with CRAFT as with Al-Anon or Nar-Anon approaches (67 against 18 in 100). Family members' own mood and family life improved in every group, whether or not their relative started treatment, but with no group left without help, no approach can take the credit. Three of the four trials came from the teams behind CRAFT, the trials counted only whether treatment started, not whether drinking or drug use changed, and families living with violence were left out of the biggest trial.
population: Family members (spouses, partners, parents and other relatives; 88–100% women across trials; aged 19 to 81) of adults with alcohol problems (two trials) or illicit drug use, cocaine most often (two trials), who refused treatment, in four US randomized trials published 1986–2002 (264 family members). In the largest trial, 130 family members in Albuquerque, New Mexico (91% women; 59% spouses, 30% parents; recruited mostly through local news media), living with the relative and seeing them on at least 40% of days; relatives with recent violence, injecting or crack cocaine use, or a more severe illicit drug problem were excluded

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say how often stopping benzodiazepines suddenly leads to seizures or other severe withdrawal reactions, or how much stopping gradually lowers that risk. As described second-hand in two narrative reviews (Lader, 2011, a descriptive review based on a lecture; Brett & Murnion, 2015, a four-page clinical review for prescribers that cites the 2011 review elsewhere), stopping or cutting down after regular use can bring a withdrawal syndrome: the 2011 review says withdrawal symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use but only in about 15 to 30 in 100 patients, a figure cited to the author's own 1998 review of stopping sleeping pills, and that rebound (the original symptoms returning more strongly for a while) is likely when stopping sleeping pills, especially short-acting ones, even after a few nights of use; the 2015 review states, without a reference, that anyone who has taken a benzodiazepine for longer than 3 to 4 weeks is likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly. Symptoms listed include anxiety and panic, poor sleep and nightmares, poor memory and concentration, low mood, muscle spasms and aches, numbness and tingling, sweating, and heightened sensitivity to light, sound and touch, with feelings of unreality; the 2011 review says they generally fade within weeks or months, often fluctuating, and both reviews say they can resemble the anxiety or insomnia the drug was taken for. Both reviews describe seizures. The 2011 review lists convulsions, delirium, psychosis, severe depression and suicidal thoughts among reactions that may follow abrupt stopping but may also occur despite slow tapering, in a table sourced to a university guide and the author's 1984 monograph, says many of them are reported anecdotally, with few case series, and that their status remains controversial; it adds that whether withdrawal occurs is related to high doses and long treatment but its severity less closely, and that severe withdrawal may occur despite withdrawal over months or years. The 2015 review states, without a reference or a frequency, that abrupt stopping after 1 to 6 months of use can cause life-threatening seizures, lists grand mal seizures 1 to 12 days after stopping in a box without a source, and describes people without a history of seizures, unstable medical or psychiatric illness or other drug dependence as at lower risk of harm from withdrawal, also without references. The only count of seizures in either review comes from a 1961 study in which 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months were switched to a dummy pill: within 2 to 8 days, 10 developed withdrawal reactions, including depression, psychosis and agitation, and 2 had seizures. Neither review cites a study comparing sudden with gradual stopping for seizures; the 2011 review says the rate at which doses are reduced rests on prescribers' clinical experience rather than good evidence, and that after high-dose use outside medical care withdrawal can sometimes be severe, with fits and psychotic reactions. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Is it dangerous to stop benzos suddenly? It can be, but the two expert reviews read here, which are not new studies, don't say how often. They describe withdrawal after regular use. One says symptoms can follow 4 to 6 weeks of use in about 15 to 30 in 100 people, a figure from the author's own earlier review, and that sleeping pills can bring back worse sleep for a while even after a few nights. Symptoms include anxiety, poor sleep, aches, tingling and sensitivity to light and sound, and they can feel like the problem the pills were taken for. Both reviews warn of seizures after stopping suddenly, and one says severe reactions can happen even with slow tapering, but it calls most reports anecdotes, the other gives no source for its seizure warning, and neither gives a rate. The only count is from 1961: 2 of 11 prisoners who had taken very high doses for months had seizures after being switched to a dummy pill.
population: People stopping or reducing regular benzodiazepine use (prescribed anxiolytics and sleeping pills, and high-dose use outside medical care), as described in two narrative reviews; in the one study with a seizure count (1961, as described), 11 prisoners given chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months
exposure: Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly, or reducing or stopping them gradually, after regular use
comparator: None in the sources described; neither review cites a study comparing abrupt with gradual stopping
outcome: Withdrawal symptoms (how often, which, how long), rebound, and severe reactions including seizures, delirium, psychosis and suicidal thoughts
magnitude: Not estimable for seizures or other severe reactions: neither review gives a frequency. As described: withdrawal symptoms after 4–6 weeks of use in about 15–30% of patients (Lader, 2011, citing Lader, 1998, ref. 124). 1961 study (Hollister et al., as described): 11 prisoners, chlordiazepoxide at several times the usual dose for several months, switched to placebo; 10 had withdrawal reactions within 2–8 days and 2 had seizures. The seizure statements in Brett & Murnion (2015) carry no references.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether police or drug detection ('sniffer') dogs at outdoor music festivals change whether people use, carry, buy or supply drugs there: the one study read measured what people said they would do in written scenarios, not what they did (Hughes et al., 2017). In a national online survey in late 2015 of 2,115 Australians aged 18 or over who had been to an outdoor music festival in the past year (mean age 22; recruited mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media; 89 in 100 had ever used an illicit drug and 78 in 100 recently), each person was assigned at random, by block, to two scenarios for a festival of 30,000 people; by the paper's paired analysis, one with no police and one of four policing scenarios: high-visibility policing (over 200 police), riot policing (over 400, including riot squads and mounted police), three sniffer dogs at the gates, or police working with health services. With any police, 72.8 in 100 said they would commit some drug offence, against 77.4 in 100 with no police; 69.6 against 76.5 said they would use drugs and 52.6 against 62.8 that they would carry drugs into the grounds, while 39.5 against 36.8 said they would buy drugs inside the grounds; stated giving and selling fell slightly (26.9 against 28.9; 3.5 against 5.1). With sniffer dogs, 66.3 in 100 said they would use drugs and 47.1 that they would carry them in; with police working with health services, 75.1 and 59.4, close to no police. About two in three said they would use drugs under every policing scenario, close to the 65.3 in 100 who said they had used drugs at their last festival. The strategies did not differ significantly in stated buying (43.8 in 100 with dogs; p = 0.711), so the paper's statement that dogs led to the most buying is not supported by its own test. The paper set significance at 0.001 but treats larger p values as significant, prints test results for giving and selling that differ between its text and table, and reports regression results whose outcome does not match its percentages (by the editors' calculation, the odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing are about 1.36, not the printed 2.69), so only the percentages are used here. The order of the two scenarios is not reported; the sample chose to take part, so the figures describe it, not festival-goers in general; and drug types and amounts were collected but not analysed, so the study says nothing about how much people would take, or about the hurried taking of drugs to avoid detection, a concern the paper cites from other sources. The authors suggest that buying inside the grounds could raise the risk of taking adulterated or mislabelled drugs, which the survey did not measure. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do police and sniffer dogs at festivals stop people taking drugs? Not by much, going by what people said, and nobody measured what they actually did. In an Australian online survey, 2,115 festival-goers, most of whom had used drugs, read made-up festival scenarios with and without police. With no police, 77 in 100 said they would use drugs; with sniffer dogs, 66 in 100 still said they would, and with police working alongside health services, 75 in 100. Fewer said they would carry drugs in when dogs were there (47 against 63 in 100), but slightly more said they would buy drugs inside the festival when any police were there (40 against 37 in 100); the authors worry those drugs may not be what they are sold as, which the survey did not check. These are intentions in imagined situations, from people who chose to answer, and some of the paper's statistics don't add up. The survey did not ask how much people would take.
population: 2,115 people aged 18 or over living in Australia who had been to at least one outdoor music festival and one licensed entertainment precinct in the past year, recruited online in late 2015 mainly through youth, music and drug forums and social media (mean age 22.3; 54.9% men; 89.1% lifetime and 78.4% recent illicit drug use; 47.0% ever stopped by police); 506 to 561 per randomized block
exposure: Written scenarios of policing at a 30,000-person outdoor festival: high-visibility policing (over 200 uniformed and plain-clothes police inside and outside), riot policing (over 400 police including public order and riot squads and mounted police), three drug detection dogs at the gates, or collaborative policing (police working with health organisations, first-aid tents and volunteers)
comparator: A written scenario with no police present, answered by the same people (order not reported); between strategies, the randomized blocks
outcome: Stated intention (yes or no) to use illicit drugs, carry them into the grounds, buy them inside, give them to a friend inside or sell them inside; perceived likelihood of detection. Actual behaviour was not measured
magnitude: Stated intentions, % (Table 4). Any police against no police: any offence 72.8 against 77.4 (−4.6 points; McNemar χ²(1) = 61.172, p < 0.001); use 69.6 against 76.5 (−6.9; χ²(1) = 102.063, p < 0.001); carry in 52.6 against 62.8 (−10.2; χ²(1) = 157.228, p < 0.001); buy inside 39.5 against 36.8 (+2.7; p = 0.001 in the text, < 0.001 in the table); give 26.9 against 28.9; sell 3.5 against 5.1 (p values differ between text and table). By strategy (high-visibility, riot, dogs, collaborative): use 67.9, 69.2, 66.3, 75.1 (p < 0.001); carry 51.7, 52.0, 47.1, 59.4 (p < 0.001); buy 38.3, 37.9, 43.8, 38.2 (p = 0.711); any offence 70.6, 72.7, 71.2, 76.6 (p = 0.003, above the paper's own 0.001 threshold). Detection judged likely or very likely for use or possession: dogs 52.3%, riot 32.9%, high-visibility 26.5%, collaborative 14.9%, no police 1.8%. Last festival (self-report): 65.3% used illicit drugs, 22.5% sold or gave drugs, 71.2% saw police. Regression odds ratios not used: editors' calculation from Table 4, odds of not offending under high-visibility against collaborative policing = (29.4/70.6)/(23.4/76.6) = 1.36 (of offending 0.73), against the printed 2.687.
